item.title: Core Concepts
item.description:
The parts of Joulie and the control loop that ties them together. Read it before the Quickstart.

What Joulie is

Joulie is a Kubernetes-native energy management system that keeps a digital twin of every managed node. The twin is fed by telemetry: CPU and GPU power read from Prometheus as the OpenTelemetry hardware metrics hw.energy and hw.power or as Kepler energy counters, and per-pod utilization from cAdvisor. It drives two outcomes: power caps and governor presets that the node agent enforces (RAPL, NVML), and scheduling, where the scheduler extender steers new pods toward the nodes with the best energy and performance trade-off.

item.title: Quickstart
item.description:
Install Joulie on a cluster and check that it manages your nodes. New to Joulie? Read Core Concepts first, or try it with only Docker in the Tutorials.

Prerequisites

  • Kubernetes with Node Feature Discovery (NFD) deployed.
  • Prometheus at http://prometheus-operated.monitoring:9090 with its OTLP receiver on (--web.enable-otlp-receiver), receiving hw.energy or hw.power for each node. values/prometheus-grafana.yaml configures kube-prometheus-stack this way (Prometheus settings), and examples/04-otel-collector-bridge converts Kepler, dcgm-exporter and AMD device-metrics-exporter metrics into those names.
  • Without that data every node reads 0 W (source prometheus-no-data). To run without Prometheus, set controllerManager.env.NODE_POWER_SOURCE=static.
  • Optional, for real enforcement: writable RAPL power limit files or cpufreq sysfs on the nodes, and NVML for NVIDIA GPUs.

Install

helm upgrade --install joulie oci://registry.cern.ch/joulie/joulie \
 --version <version> \
 -n joulie-system \
 --create-namespace \
 -f values/joulie.yaml

Upgrading an existing release? helm upgrade never updates CRDs: apply the new ones first, as Upgrading shows.

item.title: Tutorials
item.description:
Six tutorials take you from a first install to the main features, each a directory under examples/ with a README to follow. The first three run on the simulated cluster, the real Joulie components managing ten emulated bare-metal nodes in one Docker container, so start there even before a real install.

Tutorial What you will see Needs
01 Simulated cluster A first install; the hardware the agent discovers (NodeHardware); the digital twin (NodeTwin); power profiles turned into RAPL and GPU caps, down to the files the agent writes; capping a node by hand; kubectl joulie on a live workload Docker, Go, kubectl, helm, jq
02 Workload classes Performance and standard pods; the scheduler extender keeping performance pods off eco nodes, and the scores behind each placement the cluster of 01
03 Grafana dashboard kube-prometheus-stack scraping Joulie, and the dashboard the chart ships the cluster of 01, or yours
04 OpenTelemetry Collector bridge Kepler, dcgm-exporter and the AMD device-metrics-exporter turned into the hw.* metrics the digital twin reads Docker
05 Governor presets CPU and GPU governor presets, a second energy dimension next to the caps, on six hardware families Docker, Go, kubectl, helm, jq
06 Cooling and PUE Cooling models and the PUE they give for a power trace, with a Modelica FMU Python, Docker

Then install Joulie on your cluster with the Quickstart. The experiments run Joulie at scale on the simulator.

item.title: Pod Compatibility for Joulie
item.description:
How to tell Joulie where a pod may run. A single pod annotation expresses its placement intent:

joulie.io/workload-class: performance | standard

The scheduler extender reads this annotation and steers pods accordingly. No node affinity rules are needed.

The controller manager labels each managed node joulie.io/power-profile (performance or eco) with its current power state. You do not need to use that label for placement: the annotation is the single source of truth for placement intent.

item.title: Agent Runtime Modes
item.description:
How the chart deploys the node agent. Pick the mode with agent.mode:

agent.mode Pods Use
daemonset (default) one pod per managed node (charts/joulie/templates/agent-daemonset.yaml) real hardware
pool a StatefulSet whose pods each run many logical per-node agents (agent-statefulset.yaml) KWOK experiments over the simulator’s HTTP API
emulated one Deployment per node of the simulated cluster (agent-emulated.yaml), reading that node’s emulated /sys and GPU tools the simulated cluster
none no agent

item.title: Configuration Reference
item.description:
Complete reference for all Joulie environment variables. These are set via Helm values or directly in the Deployment/DaemonSet manifests.

Defaults listed below are the code defaults. The Helm chart (charts/joulie/values.yaml) overrides some of them: notably, the controller manager NODE_SELECTOR defaults to joulie.io/managed=true in the chart even though the code default is node-role.kubernetes.io/worker.

Booleans. The agent, the controller manager and the simulator read every on/off variable the same way: true, 1, yes or on, and false, 0, no or off, in any case, with surrounding spaces ignored. Unset or empty means the default. Any other value keeps the default and logs one warning naming the variable, so a typo never flips a switch. The exceptions are SIM_OTEL_FILE_METRICS, OTEL_SDK_DISABLED and fakesmi’s HWEMU_UNPRIVILEGED, whose rows say how they are read.

item.title: Upgrading
item.description:
What to check when you upgrade a Joulie installation from v0.2 to v0.3. Go through the list before running helm upgrade.

Before the upgrade

  • Apply the new CRDs. helm upgrade never updates CRDs, and the API server prunes every field the installed CRD does not know, such as the governor fields. Apply them first:

    kubectl apply -f charts/joulie/crds/

    Without a checkout, take them from the release chart: helm pull oci://registry.cern.ch/joulie/joulie --version <version> --untar --untardir /tmp/joulie-chart, then kubectl apply -f /tmp/joulie-chart/joulie/crds/.

item.title: Alerts and Runbooks
item.description:
The Joulie chart ships four alerting rules for the failures that leave a cluster looking managed while it is not: a cap that did not apply, an agent that cannot write its status, a stale digital twin, and nodes without measured power. Each has a runbook below that an operator, or an SRE agent, can follow step by step.

Installing the rules
